name: Liechtenstein
blurb: Three centuries of princes, from Vienna palaces to Vaduz Castle
dateConvention: Dates are Gregorian. The family were princes from 1608, but the principality itself was created in 1719; the deck starts with the prince reigning then. Since 2004 the heir has ruled day to day as regent for his father.

reigns.tagline: The royal tutor who got a country named after his family
reigns.cameToPower: His nephew handed him the title
reigns.previously: Princes since 1608, they bought two Alpine specks to earn a seat.
paragraphs: The Liechtensteins were filthy rich, with vast estates in Austria and Moravia. In 1608 the Habsburgs made Karl I a prince. There was a catch. To sit in the Imperial Diet, a prince needed land held straight from the emperor. So Hans-Adam I went shopping and bought the Lordship of Schellenberg in 1699 and the County of Vaduz in 1712: two little patches of Alpine valley, far from anywhere the family actually lived.

Anton Florian was the ultimate insider. He had been chief tutor to the young Archduke Charles and followed him to Spain when Charles fought for the Spanish throne. Charles lost Spain but became Emperor Charles VI in 1711, and he did not forget his old teacher. Anton Florian ran the imperial household in Vienna and sat at the heart of government.

On 23 January 1719 the emperor fused Vaduz and Schellenberg into a brand-new Principality of Liechtenstein, named after the family. Anton Florian took his seat among the princes of the Empire. He never moved there, of course. He died in Vienna in October 1721, and his son inherited a country nobody in the family had much reason to visit.

claims.text: Charles VI created the Principality of Liechtenstein on 23 January 1719.
claims.note: The imperial charter survives; the date is still marked as the country's founding.

claims.text: Anton Florian never set foot in the principality named after his family.
claims.note: Widely repeated, and there is no record of a visit, but absence of a record is not proof. The first documented visit by a reigning prince comes in 1842.

claims.text: The family bought Vaduz and Schellenberg purely to get a seat in the Imperial Diet.
claims.note: Historians agree the status was the point: the lands were small and brought in little income.

reigns.hook: Liechtenstein now exists, on paper and on the map. Anton Florian's son Joseph Johann Adam inherits it, and he lives in Vienna and Moravia, hundreds of miles away. He will run it by letter.

reigns.tagline: Four weddings, one heir, and a principality by post
reigns.previously: Anton Florian, founder of the principality, dies in Vienna.
paragraphs: Joseph Johann Adam was the second Prince of Liechtenstein and the first to inherit the brand-new country. He also inherited a stack of grander titles. He was Duke of Troppau and Jägerndorf in Silesia, owned huge estates in Moravia and Austria, and lived like it. Vaduz and Schellenberg, the bit that carried the family name, sat hundreds of miles away in the Alps.

His big worry was an heir. He married four times, and his wives kept dying young. The son he needed, Johann Nepomuk Karl, finally arrived in July 1724. Meanwhile the principality was run by officials who sent their reports to Vienna and Moravia, and the prince stayed put.
He died at Valtice, the family's Moravian seat, in December 1732, aged 42. His long-awaited heir was just eight years old.

claims.text: Joseph Johann Adam married four times.
claims.note: The family genealogies list four wives; three of them died before he did.

claims.text: He never visited Vaduz or Schellenberg as prince.
claims.note: No visit is recorded, and the first documented visit by a reigning prince is in 1842, but the 18th-century record is thin.

reigns.hook: An eight-year-old prince needs a grown-up. The job goes to his father's cousin Joseph Wenzel, a soldier and diplomat who once owned Vaduz himself.

reigns.tagline: The boy prince who ran out of time
reigns.previously: Joseph Johann Adam dies, leaving an eight-year-old heir.
paragraphs: Johann Nepomuk Karl became prince at eight, so somebody else did the ruling. That was Joseph Wenzel, his father's cousin, who acted as his guardian and ran the family's affairs from 1732 to 1745. Joseph Wenzel was a busy man at the same time, serving as the emperor's ambassador and climbing the ranks of the Austrian army.

The young prince came of age, and in 1744 he married Countess Maria Josepha of Harrach. It looked like the line was safe. It wasn't. He died at Wischau in Moravia on 22 December 1748, aged just 24, with no son to follow him.
So the title went back up the family tree, to the very man who had been minding it during his childhood.

claims.text: Joseph Wenzel served as the boy's guardian from 1732 to 1745.
claims.note: The guardianship is recorded in the standard family histories and the Historisches Lexikon.

claims.text: Johann Nepomuk Karl never saw his principality.
claims.note: No visit is recorded, but that is an argument from silence.

reigns.hook: The title goes back to Joseph Wenzel. He held Vaduz once before, swapped it away, and is now one of Austria's best generals. He's about to spend a fortune on guns.

reigns.tagline: The gunner prince who got the job twice
reigns.previously: Johann Nepomuk Karl dies at 24. His old guardian takes the title.
paragraphs: Joseph Wenzel had owned Vaduz and Schellenberg once already, as a young man from 1712. In 1718 he swapped them with his uncle Anton Florian for the lordship of Rumburk in Bohemia. Then he made a career: ambassador in Berlin and in Paris, where he rolled into town in a gilded coach that still survives.

He was also a real soldier. As an Austrian field marshal he beat the French and Spanish at Piacenza on 16 June 1746. As director-general of artillery he rebuilt the Habsburg guns from the ground up, with lighter cannon and trained crews, and he put a lot of his own money in. Frederick the Great's Prussians soon learned to respect Austrian gunfire.
In 1760 he led the glittering embassy that fetched Isabella of Parma to be the bride of the future Joseph II. He had no surviving children and died in Vienna in 1772, aged 75.

claims.text: Joseph Wenzel paid for much of the Austrian artillery reform out of his own pocket.
claims.note: Standard accounts say he spent heavily from his own fortune; how much, and how much was later repaid, is not clear.

claims.text: His golden state coach, made in Paris for his embassy there, still survives.
claims.note: The Golden Carriage is in the Princely Collections of Liechtenstein and is dated to around 1738.

claims.text: He won the Battle of Piacenza on 16 June 1746.
claims.note: He commanded the Austrian army in the battle, a heavy defeat for the Franco-Spanish force.

reigns.hook: The old marshal leaves no son. The title passes to his nephew Franz Joseph, born in Milan, who has spent years in his famous uncle's shadow.

reigns.tagline: The quiet nephew between two big personalities
reigns.previously: Joseph Wenzel I, the gunner prince, dies in Vienna without a son.
paragraphs: Franz Joseph was born in Milan in 1726, the son of Joseph Wenzel's younger brother Emanuel. He grew up as the heir to a famous uncle and spent decades waiting. He married Countess Leopoldine of Sternberg in 1750, and they had a big family.

When he finally became prince in 1772 he was 45, and his reign was short and calm. Maria Theresa still ruled in Vienna. The principality in the Alps carried on as before, run by officials and visited by nobody important.
He died at Metz on 18 August 1781, aged 54. His real legacy was his sons: two of them, Aloys and Johann, would each wear the prince's title.

claims.text: Two of his sons became reigning princes.
claims.note: Aloys I (1781–1805) and Johann I Joseph (1805–1836) were both his sons.

reigns.hook: His eldest son Aloys is only 22, and he loves books, gardens and building. The bills are about to get bigger.

reigns.tagline: The book-loving builder with no son
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest surviving son of Franz Joseph I
reigns.previously: Franz Joseph I dies at Metz. His son Aloys, 22, inherits.
paragraphs: Aloys became prince at 22. In 1783 he married Countess Karoline of Manderscheid-Blankenheim. He was a collector and a builder, and he poured money into the great family estates at Lednice and Valtice in Moravia and into the family library.

Outside the palace gates, Europe was on fire. The French Revolution turned into a long war, and in 1799 French and Austrian armies fought over the Alpine passes near the principality. Vaduz was far from Aloys's mind. He governed it, like everyone before him, from a desk hundreds of miles away.
He died in Vienna on 24 March 1805, aged 45, with no children. The title went to his younger brother Johann, a cavalry general.

claims.text: Aloys I greatly expanded the family library and the gardens at Lednice.
claims.note: Standard histories of the Lednice–Valtice estates credit him with major works there; details of costs vary.

claims.text: Liechtenstein was overrun by troops during the 1799 campaign.
claims.note: French and Austrian forces fought nearby around Feldkirch in 1799; how much the principality itself suffered is described differently by different writers.

reigns.hook: The new prince is a cavalry general, and 1805 is a terrible year to be one. Napoleon is marching on Vienna, and Johann will soon be face to face with him.

reigns.tagline: The general whose country Napoleon set free
reigns.previously: Aloys I dies without a son. His soldier brother takes the title.
paragraphs: Johann was a career cavalryman who rose to field marshal in the Austrian army. He became prince in March 1805, and that December he was at Austerlitz, where Napoleon smashed the Austrians and Russians. Afterwards Johann was one of the men sent to talk terms with the French emperor.

Then Napoleon did something strange. In 1806 he put Liechtenstein into his new Confederation of the Rhine. When the Holy Roman Empire collapsed weeks later, the little principality was suddenly a sovereign state. Its prince, meanwhile, was still a loyal Austrian general who fought Napoleon again in 1809.

After Napoleon fell, Liechtenstein joined the German Confederation in 1815, and Johann granted a first, limited constitution in 1818. He still governed from Vienna, where he spent heavily on the family estates. He died there in 1836.

claims.text: Johann negotiated face to face with Napoleon after Austerlitz.
claims.note: He took part in the armistice talks of December 1805; how much he shaped the outcome is debated.

claims.text: Johann did not welcome the sovereignty Napoleon handed him.
claims.note: His loyalty lay with Austria, and some accounts say he passed the principality on paper to his young son Karl to keep his Austrian career. Historians differ on how formal that was.

claims.text: Napoleon spared Liechtenstein out of personal regard for Johann.
claims.note: A popular explanation with no firm evidence. Plenty of small states were added to the Confederation for reasons of map-making.

reigns.hook: Johann's son is a courtier, a builder and a big spender. He will do something no reigning Liechtenstein prince has ever been recorded doing: go and look at the place.

reigns.tagline: The first prince who actually came to visit
reigns.previously: Johann I, general and reluctant sovereign, dies in Vienna.
paragraphs: More than a century after the principality was created, a reigning prince finally turned up. In 1842 Aloys II travelled to Liechtenstein and saw his subjects in person. It was a gesture, and the people noticed, but he went back to Vienna afterwards like everyone before him.

The revolutions of 1848 reached even Vaduz. Villagers demanded a say in their own affairs, and Liechtenstein sent its own delegate, Peter Kaiser, to the German parliament in Frankfurt. Aloys made some concessions, then clawed most of them back once the storm passed. In 1852 a customs treaty with Austria tied the little economy firmly to its big neighbour.

At home Aloys spent lavishly. He had Lednice rebuilt as a romantic Gothic castle and redecorated the family palaces in Vienna in high style. He died at Lednice in November 1858, leaving the title to an 18-year-old son.

claims.text: Aloys II was the first reigning prince to visit Liechtenstein.
claims.note: His 1842 visit is the first one recorded. Earlier princes may have passed through unrecorded, but no evidence of it survives.

claims.text: The 1852 customs treaty bound Liechtenstein's economy to Austria.
claims.note: The treaty put the principality inside the Austrian customs area until the First World War.

reigns.hook: The new prince is a shy teenager who loves paintings. Nobody expects much. He is about to reign for seventy years.

reigns.tagline: Seventy years on the throne, and a tiny army that grew
reigns.previously: Aloys II, the first prince to visit, dies at Lednice.
paragraphs: Johann became prince at 18 and was still prince at 88. He never married. His great love was art: he collected on a huge scale and gave away masterpieces to museums across Central Europe. His people called him Johann the Good. In 1862 he gave Liechtenstein a proper constitution with an elected parliament.

In 1866 Liechtenstein's army, all 80 men of it, marched off to guard an Alpine pass for Austria in the war against Prussia and Italy. They saw no fighting. Two years later the army was disbanded, and it has never come back. In the First World War the principality stayed neutral.

Austria came out of that war broken and broke. Liechtenstein turned to Switzerland instead. A new constitution arrived on 5 October 1921, a customs union with the Swiss in 1923 and the Swiss franc in 1924. Johann died in 1929 at Valtice, by then in Czechoslovakia.

claims.text: The army of 80 men came home from the 1866 war with 81.
claims.note: A much-loved story; the extra man is said to be an Austrian liaison officer or a new friend. Nothing official confirms the head count.

claims.text: His reign of 70 years is among the longest in European history.
claims.note: Long counted second only to Louis XIV of France; Elizabeth II of the UK passed it in 2022, so it now ranks third.

reigns.hook: Johann leaves no children. The title goes to his younger brother, a 75-year-old former ambassador whose marriage Johann would never accept.

reigns.tagline: Prince at 75, then the Nazis came to the border
reigns.previously: Johann the Good dies after 70 years, with no children.
paragraphs: Franz had waited a very long time. He had been Austria's ambassador to Russia, and he had fallen for Elsa von Gutmann, a rich widow from a Jewish family. His brother Johann would not accept the match. Once Franz was prince, at 75, he married her: quietly first, then publicly, in 1929.

In March 1938 Nazi Germany swallowed Austria, and suddenly Hitler's Reich stood on Liechtenstein's border. Local Nazis started looking across it for help. Franz's wife made him a target for their propaganda. On 31 March 1938 he named his grand-nephew Franz Joseph as regent and stepped back. He died that July at Valtice.

claims.text: Johann II refused to accept Franz's relationship with Elsa von Gutmann.
claims.note: The couple married only after Johann's death, which historians link to his opposition.

claims.text: Franz handed power to a regent because of the Nazi threat to his wife.
claims.note: Her background was a real target for local Nazis, but Franz was also 84 years old. Historians weigh the reasons differently.

reigns.hook: The new prince is 31, and he does something none of his ancestors ever did: he moves into the castle above Vaduz and stays there.

reigns.tagline: The prince who moved in and made it rich
reigns.previously: Old Franz I hands power to his grand-nephew and dies that summer.
paragraphs: Franz Joseph was the first reigning prince to live in Liechtenstein full time, in Vaduz Castle. He arrived just in time for a crisis. In March 1939 local Nazis tried a coup, hoping German troops would follow. It fizzled. Through the Second World War the principality kept its head down and stayed neutral.

In May 1945 about 500 Russian soldiers who had fought on the German side crossed the border. The Soviets wanted them back, which for many meant death. Tiny Liechtenstein said no and gave them asylum. The war cost the family dearly: Czechoslovakia seized its huge estates. In 1967 Franz Joseph sold Leonardo's “Ginevra de' Benci” to the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

After the war came the boom. Industry and finance turned a poor farming country into one of the richest on earth. Women finally won the vote in 1984. That August, Franz Joseph handed day-to-day rule to his son Hans-Adam. He died in office in November 1989, after 51 years.

claims.text: Liechtenstein refused to hand about 500 Russian soldiers to the Soviet Union in 1945.
claims.note: Well documented; a memorial at Hinterschellenberg marks where they crossed the border.

claims.text: Ginevra de' Benci is the only painting by Leonardo in the Americas.
claims.note: The National Gallery of Art says so; it bought the painting from the princely collection in 1967.

claims.text: The 1939 coup failed partly because Hitler did not want it.
claims.note: German forces did not move to support the plotters, but how far Berlin ever backed them is debated.

reigns.hook: The new prince is a banker who rebuilt the family fortune with his own hands. Now he has a plan for the constitution, and it gives the prince a lot more power.

reigns.tagline: The banker prince who asked for more power and got it
reigns.previously: Franz Joseph II dies after 51 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Hans-Adam studied business at St Gallen and then took charge of the family's money. He turned LGT, the family bank, from a small local lender into an international group, rebuilding a fortune the war had shattered. He took over day-to-day rule in 1984 and became prince in 1989. In 1990 Liechtenstein joined the United Nations.

Most modern monarchs give up power. Hans-Adam went looking for it. In 2003 he put constitutional changes to the voters that confirmed the prince's veto over laws and let him dismiss the government. He said the family would leave the country if he lost. About 64% voted yes. In 2012 voters rejected a proposal to curb the prince's veto.

On 15 August 2004 he handed day-to-day rule to his son Alois as regent, while staying head of state. That is how things still stand: Hans-Adam is the reigning prince, and Alois does the daily work of ruling.

claims.text: Hans-Adam threatened to leave Liechtenstein if he lost the 2003 referendum.
claims.note: Widely reported at the time, including by the BBC; he spoke of moving to Vienna.

claims.text: The 2003 referendum passed with about 64% in favour.
claims.note: Official result: 64.3% yes in the vote of March 2003.

claims.text: In 2012 about three-quarters of voters backed keeping the prince's veto.
claims.note: Official result of the July 2012 referendum, reported by the BBC.
